title: Three weeks on the ice, and what the sensors missed
intro: A diary from the spring campaign at the alpine station: what worked, what froze, and the two days we threw away.

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: We arrived on a Sunday with four cases of instruments and left three weeks later with two of them still working. This is the honest version of the campaign — including the part where the calibration drift made the first week's data unusable.

add_image.image_alt: The station building under a clear sky
add_image.image_caption: The station at 06:40, before the first run.

add_heading.heading_text: What we set out to do

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: The plan was simple: continuous particulate sampling at three heights, a daily snow pit, and a calibration check every morning. The first two happened. The third became the story.

add_focus_list.heading: In numbers
items_of_the_focus_list: 21 days on site, 18 with usable weather.
2 days of data discarded after calibration drift.

images.image_alt: Instruments set up on the snow
images.image_caption: The upper sampling mast on day two.

images.image_alt: A snow pit with marked layers
images.image_caption: The daily snow pit, layers marked for density.
Last light, and the generator still running.

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph:
By day four the reference logger and the field units disagreed by 7%. We spent a day chasing a loose connector, found nothing, and eventually traced it to the housing warming faster than the reference. The fix was a shade and a longer equilibration time. The cost was the first week's particulate series.

We kept the raw files. They are not wrong, they are just not comparable, and that distinction matters more than it sounds.

add_quote.text: The instrument was fine. The instrument in a box in the sun was not.

add_special_note.heading: What we would change
add_special_note.text: Two things: shade the housings from the first day, and log the internal temperature alongside the measurement. Both are now standard in the field kit.
